title: Vance Urges Iran to Cut Nuclear Capability Significantly to End War, Fox News Reports
body:
Washington’s top officials are quietly laying the groundwork for a possible military response to Tehran, a move that appears to be timed with the looming November 3 midterm elections. According to multiple senior sources, the White House has instructed the Department of Defense to draft contingency plans for strikes against Iranian targets, while senior administration officials have signaled to allies that President Donald Trump retains “all options” in dealing with what Washington describes as a “dangerous escalation” in Tehran’s nuclear program. The push for a “meaningful reduction” in Iran’s nuclear capability, voiced by senior advisers, comes amid growing pressure from Republican congressional candidates who argue that a decisive show of force is overdue.

The directive to the Pentagon, which was reportedly conveyed in a closed‑door meeting last week, calls for a comprehensive assessment of potential strike options ranging from limited precision attacks on nuclear facilities to broader conventional operations aimed at degrading Iran’s ballistic‑missile infrastructure. Defense planners are said to be evaluating a range of scenarios, including the use of stealth aircraft, cruise missiles launched from naval vessels, and cyber‑enabled sabotage of enrichment centrifuges. While no decision has been made, the preparation of these plans signals a shift from diplomatic engagement to a posture that leaves open the possibility of kinetic action.

Republican hopefuls in the House of Representatives have seized on the issue, framing the perceived inaction of previous administrations as a failure to confront a longstanding threat. Dan Green, a GOP candidate for a swing district in Ohio, told local media that the conflict with Iran “did not begin with a single incident; it is the culmination of a decades‑long pattern of aggression that started with the 1979 hostage crisis.” Green, a former Army officer, argues that a robust military response would not only curb Iran’s nuclear ambitions but also restore American credibility in the Middle East. Other candidates across the country echo his sentiment, suggesting that a decisive strike could rally the party’s base and influence voter sentiment ahead of the midterms.

Critics, however, warn that the timing and rhetoric risk inflaming an already volatile region. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps has repeatedly warned that any attack on its nuclear facilities would be met with “proportionate retaliation,” a phrase that could encompass attacks on U.S. bases in the Gulf, commercial shipping, or even cyber‑attacks on critical infrastructure. Regional allies such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have expressed concern that an American strike could destabilize oil markets and trigger a broader conflagration involving proxy militias in Iraq, Syria and Yemen. Diplomatic channels, including back‑channel talks in Vienna and Geneva, continue to operate, but their effectiveness is hampered by mutual distrust and Tehran’s insistence on “full sovereignty” over its nuclear program.

The broader strategic calculus also involves the domestic political landscape. With the midterms poised to determine control of both chambers of Congress, the administration’s handling of Iran could become a pivotal campaign issue. Democrats have criticized the administration for “playing politics with war,” while some Republicans argue that a strong stance could boost national security credentials. Meanwhile, intelligence officials caution that premature military action could undermine ongoing negotiations and give Iran a pretext to accelerate its enrichment activities, potentially pushing it closer to the 20 percent weapons‑grade threshold that would trigger automatic sanctions under the 2015 nuclear deal framework.

As the United States navigates this precarious juncture, the next steps will likely hinge on a blend of diplomatic pressure, economic sanctions and the readiness of the military to act if deemed necessary. The administration has not ruled out a diplomatic solution, but the preparation of strike options underscores a willingness to consider force if Tehran does not curtail its nuclear advancements. Observers note that any move—whether a limited strike or a broader campaign—will have far‑reaching implications for regional stability, global energy markets and the United States’ standing on the world stage. The coming weeks will reveal whether Washington chooses to press the button or to double down on negotiations, a decision that will shape U.S.–Iran relations for years to come.
